intro: The Loan Eligibility Calculator estimates the maximum loan amount a bank is likely to offer you, based on your monthly income, existing EMIs, interest rate, and tenure.
uses: It is used before applying for a home loan, car loan, or personal loan to find a realistic borrowing limit, and to see how paying off an existing EMI or choosing a longer tenure changes that limit.
formula: Maximum EMI you can afford = (Monthly Income × 50%) − Existing Monthly EMIs. Maximum loan = Max EMI × ((1+r)^n − 1) ÷ (r × (1+r)^n), where r is the monthly interest rate (annual rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100) and n is the tenure in months. This uses the 50% FOIR (Fixed Obligation to Income Ratio) rule most Indian banks apply.
example: Inputs: Monthly Income = ₹50,000, Monthly EMI Obligations = ₹5,000, Annual Interest Rate = 8.5%, Loan Tenure = 20 years. Step 1: maximum EMI = 50,000 × 50% − 5,000 = ₹20,000. Step 2: monthly rate r = 8.5 ÷ 12 ÷ 100 = 0.007083, n = 240 months. Step 3: maximum loan = 20,000 × ((1.007083)^240 − 1) ÷ (0.007083 × (1.007083)^240) = ₹23,04,617.
howTo: Step 1: Enter your monthly income in the "Monthly Income (₹)" field.
Step 2: Enter all EMIs you already pay each month in the "Monthly EMI Obligations (₹)" field.
Step 3: Enter the expected annual interest rate in the "Annual Interest Rate (%)" field.
Step 4: Enter the repayment period in the "Loan Tenure (Years)" field.
Step 5: Tap Calculate to see the maximum loan amount and the maximum EMI allowed.
tips: Paying off or closing an existing loan raises your eligibility more than a small salary rise, because it frees up EMI capacity directly.
A longer tenure raises the eligible amount, but it also means paying much more interest over the life of the loan.
Banks also check your credit score, job stability, and the property value — this calculator shows the income-based limit only.
Borrowing the maximum you are eligible for is not always wise; leave room in your budget for emergencies.
mistakes: Leaving out existing EMIs such as a bike loan or credit card EMI, which makes the eligible amount look higher than the bank will offer.
Entering gross salary instead of the monthly income the bank will count.
Entering the tenure in months instead of years — this calculator expects years.
Assuming the calculated amount is guaranteed — it is an estimate, and the bank's final sanction can be lower.

faqs.q: How much loan can I get on a ₹50,000 monthly income?
faqs.a: With no other EMIs at 8.5% over 20 years, the 50% FOIR rule allows a maximum EMI of ₹25,000, which supports a loan of about ₹28.8 lakh. With ₹5,000 of existing EMIs, the limit falls to about ₹23.0 lakh.

FOIR stands for Fixed Obligation to Income Ratio. Most Indian banks allow total fixed monthly obligations — all EMIs together — up to about 50% of your monthly income. This calculator uses that 50% limit.

faqs.q: Does my credit score affect loan eligibility?
faqs.a: Yes. This calculator only checks the income-based limit. Banks also look at your credit score, repayment history, employment type, and the value of the property or asset before sanctioning a loan.
